Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Michael Martin, the speaker of Britain's House of Commons, said Tuesday he would resign in the face of widespread public anger over expense claims by lawmakers. Michael Martin, the House of Commons Speaker, has tendered his resignation. Martin, whose statement lasted barely a minute, said he would step down June 21. He is the first speaker to be forced out of office since 1695. Martin said he was stepping down in order to promote "unity" in the House of Commons. Prime Minister Gordon Brown later Tuesday announced recommendations for comprehensive reforms to the expenses system to put an end to the "abuses and misjudgments of the past."  Watch how the rules have led to abuse » . He proposed a review of expense claims of the past few years by an independent panel, and the introduction of an outside agency to regulate expense reimbursements, which Parliament currently does itself. Parliament at "Westminster cannot operate like some gentlemen's club," he said. "There has got to be transparency. There has got to be a proper audit."  Watch more of Brown's speech » . The reforms are currently only proposals. It is not clear if they will be implemented. Brown also paid tribute to Martin and added that he had chaired a meeting of party leaders Tuesday afternoon to discuss an overhaul of the expenses system. The speaker traditionally chairs debates and ensures protocol is followed. But part of the reason MPs are now focusing their anger on Martin is that his office also handles expense claims.  Watch more on Martin's resignation » . Critics say he allowed claims to run amok and failed to recognize the depth of public disgust at the amounts being claimed -- into the tens of thousands of dollars for some lawmakers. Martin was savaged by MPs on Monday after he addressed parliament, with one lawmaker after another demanding to know when he would resign. Politicians across the political spectrum have been under fire after weeks of front-page headlines revealing their expense claims. What do you think about the expense scandal? They included requests for reimbursements for mortgages that had been paid off, members of the same family claiming the same expenses and reimbursement for lavish home furnishings. The justice minister, Shahid Malik, resigned from the Cabinet over his claims, which he insisted were within the allowable limits. The governing Labour Party also cut ties with MP Elliot Morley, a former Cabinet minister, over his expense claims.  Watch London cabbies speak out against lawmakers » . The expenses scandal came to light in a series of recent front-page reports in The Daily Telegraph newspaper. The expense claims were to be made public in the summer, but the Telegraph obtained them early. Many lawmakers put in the spotlight by the newspaper insist they broke no rules. London's Metropolitan Police announced shortly before Martin's resignation that they would not investigate the leaking of the expense reports to the press. "The leak of documents is not something that the (Metropolitan Police) would condone," they said in a statement, but felt it was unlikely they would obtain the evidence they need to launch a successful prosecution. The police had not yet decided whether to investigate whether politicians broke the law in their expense claims, the statement added.

LONDON, England (CNN) — Amid intense public outrage over lawmakers’ expense claims, Michael Martin announced Tuesday that he would leave his post as speaker of Britain’s House of Commons.

In a statement lasting less than a minute, Martin said his resignation would take effect on June 21 and that he was stepping aside to encourage “unity” within the Commons. He is the first speaker to be driven from the position since 1695.

Later Tuesday, Prime Minister Gordon Brown outlined proposals for a sweeping overhaul of the parliamentary expenses system, saying the changes were intended to end the “abuses and misjudgments of the past.” His recommendations included having an independent panel examine claims submitted over the previous several years and creating an external body to oversee expense repayments, a responsibility currently managed by Parliament itself.

Brown said Westminster could no longer function “like some gentlemen’s club,” adding: “There has got to be transparency. There has got to be a proper audit.”

The suggested reforms have not yet been adopted, and it remains uncertain whether they will take effect. Brown also praised Martin and said he had led a meeting of party leaders Tuesday afternoon to consider restructuring the expenses system.

The speaker’s customary responsibilities include presiding over debates and making sure parliamentary procedures are observed. However, Martin became a particular target of MPs’ anger because his office was also responsible for processing expense claims.

His critics accused him of allowing the system to spiral out of control and of failing to appreciate the scale of public revulsion over claims that, for some lawmakers, reached tens of thousands of dollars. After Martin addressed Parliament on Monday, MPs attacked him sharply, with lawmakers repeatedly asking when he intended to resign.

Politicians from all parties had faced mounting criticism after several weeks of front-page stories detailing their reimbursement requests. The claims included payments toward mortgages that had already been settled, duplicate expenses submitted by members of the same family, and compensation for extravagant household furnishings.

Justice Minister Shahid Malik left the Cabinet because of questions surrounding his expenses, although he maintained that all his claims fell within permitted limits. The governing Labour Party also severed ties with MP Elliot Morley, a former Cabinet minister, over his reimbursement requests.

The controversy emerged through a series of prominent reports published by The Daily Telegraph. Although the records were scheduled for public release during the summer, the newspaper acquired them in advance. Many of the MPs identified in the coverage argued that they had not violated any rules.

Shortly before Martin announced his departure, London’s Metropolitan Police said they would not investigate how the expense documents had been leaked to the media. In a statement, police said they did not condone the disclosure but believed they were unlikely to secure enough evidence for a successful prosecution.

The statement also said that police had not yet determined whether to investigate if any politicians had broken the law through their expense claims.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about House of Commons Speaker Michael Martin resigning amid the British MPs’ expenses scandal.
counterfactuals.output:
# UK Commons speaker resigns amid expenses scandal

**LONDON, England —** House of Commons Speaker Michael Martin announced Tuesday that he will step down amid growing anger over British lawmakers’ expenses, becoming the first speaker forced from office in more than 300 years.

Martin told a packed chamber that he would resign as speaker on June 21, 2009, allowing lawmakers to elect a successor the following day. He also said he would leave Parliament as the member for Glasgow North East.

“Since I came to the House 30 years ago, I have always felt that the House is at its best when it is united,” Martin said in a brief statement. “In order that unity can be maintained, I have decided that I will relinquish the office of speaker.”

His departure followed days of intense criticism over his response to revelations that members of Parliament had claimed taxpayer-funded expenses for items ranging from home renovations and household goods to mortgage payments on properties with no outstanding loans.

Martin was accused of failing to lead efforts to reform the expenses system and of focusing instead on how details of the claims were leaked to the media. A growing number of lawmakers had signed a motion declaring they had lost confidence in him.

Prime Minister Gordon Brown paid tribute to Martin’s public service, while opposition leaders said his resignation must be followed by broader reforms to restore public trust.

The scandal, fueled by a series of reports in *The Daily Telegraph*, implicated lawmakers from all major parties. Several MPs announced plans to repay money or leave Parliament, while party leaders promised tighter oversight and greater transparency.

Martin, a former sheet-metal worker who became speaker in 2000, was the first Roman Catholic to hold the post since the Reformation. His resignation marked the first time a Commons speaker had been driven from office since Sir John Trevor was removed in 1695.

The speaker is expected to remain politically impartial while presiding over debates and representing the authority of the House of Commons. Martin’s successor will face immediate pressure to overhaul parliamentary expenses and rebuild public confidence in Britain’s political institutions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain why Michael Martin resigned as Speaker in 2009, including Gordon Brown’s proposed reforms and examples of controversial parliamentary expense claims.
counterfactuals.output:
Michael Martin resigned as Speaker of the House of Commons in May 2009 because he had lost the confidence of many MPs during the parliamentary expenses scandal.

The *Daily Telegraph*, using leaked expense records, revealed widespread misuse or aggressive exploitation of MPs’ allowances. Martin was blamed not for creating the system, but for defending the Commons’ tradition of regulating itself and for appearing more concerned with stopping leaks and protecting MPs than with achieving transparency. The Speaker’s Office had also supported efforts to resist full disclosure under freedom-of-information laws. His confrontational handling of MPs who questioned him, followed by an apology widely regarded as inadequate, intensified the criticism. A cross-party group backed a motion of no confidence, making his position untenable.

Martin announced on 19 May that he would leave office on 21 June 2009. He was the first Speaker forced from office in more than 300 years.

Examples of controversial claims included:

- **Sir Peter Viggers’s** claim for a £1,645 ornamental “duck house.”
- **Douglas Hogg’s** inclusion of the cost of cleaning the moat at his country estate in his expenses documentation.
- **Elliot Morley’s** claims for mortgage interest after the mortgage had already been repaid.
- **Jacqui Smith’s** expenses claim that included the cost of adult films watched by her husband, as well as controversy over which residence she designated as her main home.
- **Hazel Blears’s** repeated redesignation, or “flipping,” of homes, which allowed her to maximize allowances; she later repaid capital-gains tax.
- Claims by various MPs for items such as chandeliers, swimming-pool maintenance, gardening, furniture and extensive home renovations.

Prime Minister **Gordon Brown** argued that Parliament could no longer be trusted to police its own expenses. His reform proposals included:

- replacing Commons self-regulation with an **independent statutory authority** to administer and scrutinize MPs’ pay and allowances;
- independent auditing and fuller publication of claims and receipts;
- tighter rules on second homes, including ending or restricting mortgage-interest claims and preventing “flipping” for financial advantage;
- a statutory code of conduct and stronger procedures for investigating MPs;
- initially, replacing the second-home allowance with a flat-rate attendance payment—an idea derided as a “clocking-in allowance” and subsequently abandoned.

These plans led to the creation of the **Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority (IPSA)** under the Parliamentary Standards Act 2009. Martin’s resignation therefore reflected both personal criticism of his leadership and a broader collapse of public confidence in the Commons’ system of self-regulation.

# Commons Speaker Michael Martin resigns amid expenses scandal

**May 19, 2009 — London**

Michael Martin announced Tuesday that he will resign as Speaker of Britain’s House of Commons, becoming the highest-profile casualty of the parliamentary expenses scandal that has engulfed Westminster.

In a brief statement to MPs, Martin said he would leave the post next month.

> “In order that unity can be maintained, I have decided that I will relinquish the office of Speaker on Sunday 21 June,” he told the Commons.

He added:

> “This will allow the House to proceed to elect a new Speaker on Monday 22 June.”

The announcement followed mounting criticism of Martin’s handling of disclosures about MPs’ allowances and his response to demands for greater transparency. A growing number of MPs had called for him to step down, arguing that the authority of Parliament had been severely damaged.

Martin, the Labour MP for Glasgow North East, had served as Speaker since 2000. His departure will make him the first Commons Speaker in more than three centuries to be forced from office, since Sir John Trevor was expelled in 1695.

Prime Minister Gordon Brown paid tribute to Martin’s public service, telling MPs:

> “He has served this House for 30 years with distinction.”

Conservative leader David Cameron said the resignation offered Parliament an opportunity for change, but warned that replacing the Speaker alone would not resolve the crisis.

> “The problems go much wider than the Speaker,” Cameron said. “This is an opportunity for Parliament to make a clean break with the past.”

Public anger has intensified following newspaper reports detailing claims submitted by MPs for mortgages, repairs, furnishings and other costs under the parliamentary allowances system. MPs from all major parties have faced scrutiny, prompting repayments, disciplinary action and promises of sweeping reform.

Martin had initially resisted calls to resign and rebuked MPs who challenged his handling of the affair. But his position became increasingly untenable after a formal motion of no confidence attracted cross-party support.

The Commons will now prepare for its first contested election of a Speaker since Martin took office. His successor will face immediate pressure to overhaul Parliament’s expenses regime and restore public confidence in Britain’s political institutions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the UK parliamentary expenses scandal, focusing on Michael Martin’s departure, public anger, implicated politicians, and the Metropolitan Police response.
counterfactuals.output:
The UK parliamentary expenses scandal erupted in 2009 after *The Daily Telegraph* published leaked records showing MPs claiming public money for questionable costs, including second homes, mortgage interest, renovations, tax advice, moat cleaning and a “duck house.” Although many claims complied with parliamentary rules, the disclosures suggested a culture of entitlement and manipulation across party lines, provoking intense anger during a recession.

- **Michael Martin’s departure:** Commons Speaker Michael Martin was widely criticised for presiding over the expenses system, resisting disclosure and appearing more concerned with identifying the source of the leak than restoring public trust. After losing support across the House, he announced his resignation in May 2009 and left office the following month, also giving up his Glasgow North East seat. He was the first Speaker forced from office in more than 300 years.

- **Public anger:** Voters saw the claims as evidence that politicians operated under rules unavailable to ordinary people. Controversies over “flipping” designated second homes, avoiding capital-gains tax and claiming for extravagant or trivial items badly damaged confidence in Parliament. MPs faced public confrontations, repayments, deselection pressures and demands for wholesale reform.

- **Politicians implicated:** Figures from all major parties were caught up in the scandal. Prominent cases included Labour politicians Jacqui Smith, Hazel Blears, Elliot Morley, David Chaytor and Jim Devine, and Conservatives Douglas Hogg, Peter Viggers, Andrew MacKay and Julie Kirkbride. Some cases involved embarrassing but lawful claims; others involved alleged false accounting. Several MPs and peers were later convicted and imprisoned, including Morley, Chaytor, Devine and Conservative peer Lord Hanningfield.

- **Metropolitan Police response:** Scotland Yard initially resisted launching a broad criminal investigation, arguing that many disputes concerned ambiguous Commons rules rather than clear fraud. After reviewing evidence with the Crown Prosecution Service, the Metropolitan Police opened targeted investigations into cases where there appeared to be evidence of deliberate dishonesty. These investigations led to prosecutions, while most claims were handled through repayments, parliamentary discipline and reforms rather than criminal charges.

The scandal ultimately brought tighter oversight, including creation of the Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority, and fundamentally changed how MPs’ expenses were administered and published.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a detailed report beginning “LONDON, England (CNN) --” about Michael Martin becoming the first Commons speaker forced from office since 1695.
counterfactuals.output:
LONDON, England (CNN) -- Michael Martin announced Tuesday that he would step down as speaker of the House of Commons, becoming the first holder of the office to be forced out in more than 300 years.

Martin told lawmakers he would relinquish the speakership on June 21, with an election for his successor scheduled for the following day. His brief statement followed mounting criticism of his handling of the parliamentary expenses scandal that had shaken public confidence in British politics.

The speaker, who had held the post since 2000, said his departure was intended to preserve unity in the Commons. He made no detailed defense of his conduct and left the chamber shortly after the announcement.

His resignation made him the first Commons speaker driven from office since Sir John Trevor was expelled in 1695 after being found guilty of accepting a bribe.

Pressure on Martin had intensified as newspapers published details of lawmakers’ expense claims, including payments for second homes, renovations, furniture and other costs charged to taxpayers. Although anger was directed at members from all major parties, Martin was accused of failing to act decisively and of treating attempts to expose the system as attacks on Parliament.

Critics said the Commons authorities under Martin had fought too hard to prevent the disclosure of expense records. They also accused him of rebuking lawmakers who questioned his leadership rather than acknowledging the scale of public anger.

A group of members submitted a motion of no confidence, an extraordinary challenge because the speaker is traditionally regarded as politically neutral and normally remains in office until choosing to retire. While the motion itself was unlikely to be debated, it demonstrated that Martin no longer commanded the broad support needed to continue.

Prime Minister Gordon Brown paid tribute to Martin’s public service but accepted that Parliament had to change. Opposition Conservative leader David Cameron said the resignation could not, by itself, resolve the crisis and called for wider reforms to the expenses system and the way the Commons was governed.

Martin’s departure represented a dramatic fall for a politician whose election as speaker had been seen as a symbol of social mobility. Born in Glasgow and raised in a working-class family, he left school as a teenager and worked as a sheet-metal worker before becoming active in the trade union movement and entering Parliament as a Labour lawmaker in 1979.

Known to supporters and critics alike as “Gorbals Mick,” a reference to the Glasgow district associated with his upbringing, Martin became the first Roman Catholic to serve as speaker since the Reformation era. On taking the chair, he gave up his party affiliation, as required by the conventions of the office.

The speaker presides over debates, enforces parliamentary rules and represents the Commons in its dealings with the monarch, the House of Lords and other authorities. Although the position is formally nonpartisan, its authority depends heavily on the confidence of lawmakers across the political spectrum.

That confidence deteriorated rapidly during the expenses controversy. Public outrage grew as reports revealed that some members had claimed reimbursement for costs that appeared extravagant, unnecessary or only loosely connected to their parliamentary duties. Several lawmakers agreed to repay money, while party leaders promised disciplinary action and independent scrutiny.

The scandal also exposed weaknesses in a system that had largely allowed Parliament to regulate itself. Critics argued that secrecy, vague rules and a culture of entitlement had enabled questionable claims to continue for years.

Martin initially resisted calls for his resignation, insisting that he was overseeing reforms. But his position became increasingly precarious after a tense Commons appearance in which he criticized members who challenged him over the handling of the disclosures. The intervention was widely viewed as evidence that he had underestimated the depth of the crisis.

His announcement cleared the way for the first contested election for speaker in nearly a decade. Candidates were expected to face questions not only about their ability to manage debate but also about whether they would support greater transparency, stronger independent oversight and a reduction in the speaker’s administrative powers.

Martin’s resignation did not end the expenses controversy. All three major parties faced demands to remove lawmakers who had abused the system, tighten the rules and restore public trust before the next general election.

The episode marked one of the gravest institutional crises to confront the modern House of Commons. By forcing out its presiding officer for the first time since the 17th century, lawmakers acknowledged that the scandal had become not merely a dispute over individual claims but a challenge to Parliament’s credibility and authority.
